title: Why Your Family Never Pays You Back

beats.text: Dave asks his brother for three thousand dollars back. At Thanksgiving. In front of Mom. His brother says, “Wait. I thought that was a gift.”
Rewind to April. Danny's car died, so Dave sent his entire emergency fund. The contract was a pizza emoji. No due date. No repayment plan.
Then something strange happened. Danny paid his car loan, phone bill, and credit card on time. Dave got nothing. When Dave's own tire blew, he had to put four hundred dollars on a credit card.

Think of payday as a deli line. The landlord gets served first. Then the car lender, phone company, and credit card. They can charge fees or take something away. Dave can't. So Dave waits at the back, smiling.
And this isn't rare. Bankrate's 2025 survey found that among people who lent money expecting repayment, forty-four percent lost money. Twenty-six percent said the relationship was damaged.
Danny may not be a villain. He may simply be broke, with bills that punish him for paying late. But without a written plan, Dave is the easiest person to postpone.
There's another problem: the IRS says you need evidence that money was meant to be a loan, not a gift. A written note and repayment schedule help. A pizza emoji doesn't.
Dave fixes it privately. One page: three thousand dollars, one hundred twenty-five dollars a month, the day after payday, for twenty-four months. They both sign, and Danny sets an automatic transfer.

Now Dave has a date and a place in the line. Before lending money again, he asks five words: “Is this a gift, or a loan?” If it's a loan, write down the terms. If losing it would hurt, say no—or give only what you can afford as a gift. Protect the relationship before the money moves.
